opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most underrated ways to contribute, and a lot of people sort of rule themselves out because they think, "Well, I'm not a researcher, I don't have a PhD in machine learning, so there's nothing for me here." And I just think that's wrong.

The core thing to understand is that a huge amount of safety research, especially empirical work like interpretability, is bottlenecked on engineering. When I'm doing research, a lot of what I'm actually doing day to day isn't having brilliant conceptual insights. It's writing code, running experiments, waiting for things to finish, debugging infrastructure, wrangling data, figuring out why my GPU ran out of memory. The faster you can go from "I have an idea" to "I have a result," the more ideas you can test, and the research process is really just a loop of trying lots of things and seeing what works. If you can make that loop tighter, you speed everything up.

So if someone builds good tooling, say a library that makes it easy to get at a model's internal activations, or infrastructure that lets researchers run experiments at scale without each person reinventing the wheel, that has a multiplier effect. It's not just making one person faster, it's making a whole field faster. I've seen this firsthand with things like TransformerLens. A lot of people have told me that having an accessible library was what let them get started in mechanistic interpretability at all, and that kind of lowering of the barrier to entry is genuinely valuable.

The other thing is that good software engineering is just a different skill set from research, and it's often a skill set researchers don't have. Researchers tend to write hacky code because they're optimising for getting a result quickly, which is often the right call, but it means there's a lot of value in someone who actually knows how to write clean, reliable, well-tested systems. At the big labs especially, a lot of safety work depends on infrastructure for training, evaluation, and running large models efficiently, and strong engineers are a real bottleneck there.

And you don't need to understand the deep ML theory to be useful. You need to be a good engineer, be willing to learn the domain enough to understand what researchers need, and care about the mission. You'll pick up a lot of the ML along the way just by being close to the work. Honestly, a lot of strong research engineers end up drifting into research themselves because they develop such good intuitions from being in the weeds.

So my pitch would be: if you're a strong software engineer and you care about AI going well, don't assume you need to retrain as a researcher first. There's a lot of impact to be had by just being the person who makes the researchers ten times more productive.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering can speed research and describes shared tooling, but does not mention mature technology companies, small teams, or their idiosyncratic workflows.

r002.rationale: It presents strong software engineering on infrastructure for training, evaluation, and efficient large-model experiments as a way to accelerate safety research, and says deep ML theory is not required.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most underrated paths, honestly. The way I'd frame it is: what's the actual bottleneck on safety research right now? And my experience, having been inside a few of these teams, is that it's very often not ideas. There are far more promising experiments to run than there are hours to run them. The bottleneck is throughput: how fast can a researcher go from "I wonder if X is true" to actually having a plot in front of them that tells them whether X is true.

And an enormous amount of that loop is just engineering. It's infrastructure for running models, tooling for caching activations, pipelines for training things like sparse autoencoders at scale, making sure the research codebase isn't a horrible pile of spaghetti that breaks every time someone touches it. None of that requires you to have deep intuitions about mechanistic interpretability or to be able to read the latest paper and have a hot take on it. It requires you to be a good software engineer who can work with researchers and understand what they're trying to do well enough to build the right thing.

The thing I'd really emphasise is that this is a multiplier. If you're a researcher, you get maybe one researcher's worth of output. If you're an engineer who makes a team of ten researchers 20% more productive, you've just created two researchers' worth of output, and that's a pretty conservative number. I've seen cases where a single piece of good infrastructure changed what experiments were even feasible to run, and that unlocks entire research directions, not just incremental speedups.

I also think people have a slightly distorted picture where they imagine the "real" impact is in having the ideas, and engineering is somehow lower status or less important. And I just think that's wrong. The history of machine learning is substantially a history of people building better tooling and then discovering that things which used to be hard became easy. Interpretability in particular is at a stage where a lot of what we need is just to be able to run many more experiments, much faster, on much bigger models.

So if you're someone with strong software skills who cares about this stuff and is thinking, "Well, I don't have a PhD, I haven't published anything, I can't really contribute," I'd push back pretty hard. Go talk to safety teams. Ask what their researchers spend their time doing that they wish they didn't have to. You'll find there's a lot, and fixing it is extremely valuable.

r001.rationale: The response describes engineering as a way to increase research throughput, but does not mention mature technology companies, small teams, or their idiosyncratic workflows.

r002.rationale: It presents strong software engineering across research infrastructure and tooling as a way to accelerate safety research, and says this can be done without deep interpretability knowledge or expertise in reading research papers.

astra-6.text:
I think people often underestimate how much research is bottlenecked on getting things to work. Having a research idea is one part of the process, but then you need to run experiments, manage the results, build tools to inspect what happened, and iterate. A good engineer can make that whole process substantially faster.

You don’t necessarily need to be the person who knows which research question to ask. You can work closely with a researcher who has that judgment, notice where they’re spending hours doing something awkward or repetitive, and build something that makes it easy. If your work saves several researchers a significant fraction of their time, that can be a substantial contribution to the research agenda.

There’s still context you need to learn. You need to understand what the researchers are trying to do well enough to build useful things. But that’s a much more accessible starting point than needing to come in with original ideas about how to solve AI safety. Strong software engineering, good communication, and a willingness to learn can take you quite far.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering can speed experiments and iteration by improving awkward or repetitive workflows, but it does not state that mature technology companies have substantial room to improve iteration speed for small teams with idiosyncratic workflows.

r002.rationale: The response presents strong software engineering as a way to help without originating research ideas, but it does not identify proficiency in deep, complex technology stacks.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of research depends on having good tools. If you can build something that makes a researcher’s experiments easier to run, helps them understand the results, or saves them hours of repetitive work, you can make that researcher substantially more productive. And if several researchers use it, that benefit can multiply.

You don’t necessarily need to know how to come up with a promising research direction to do that. You need to be a good engineer, talk to researchers, and understand where they’re getting stuck. You’ll probably need to learn some machine learning along the way, but that’s different from needing to be an ML expert before you can contribute.

The important caveat is that you want to check that you’re solving a real problem. It’s easy to build a tool that sounds useful but nobody actually uses. So I’d start by working closely with a researcher, finding something concrete that’s slowing them down, and making that better.

r001.rationale: The response says useful tools can make researchers more productive, but does not mention mature technology companies, small teams, or their idiosyncratic workflows.

r002.rationale: The response presents engineering skill as useful without prior ML expertise, but does not identify proficiency in deep, complex technology stacks.
